items.title: That Antivirus Renewal Email Is Fake — Check Your Bank Statement First
items.summary: Scammers are emailing people a convincing receipt that says their antivirus subscription just auto-renewed for about $130, with a handy link to cancel it. There is no subscription and no charge. The cancel page is a fake form that collects your name, email address and number so a fake support agent can call you next. Don't click the link and don't fill in that form. Check your own bank statement instead — no charge means nothing to cancel.

items.title: Is your Windows 11 computer about to stop getting free security updates? Microsoft's October 13 deadline takes 30 seconds to check in Settings
items.summary: On October 13, Microsoft stops sending free security updates to the older version of Windows 11 that shipped back in 2024. The fix is free and it's just an update: open Settings > Windows Update, click Check for updates, and install everything it offers — your files and programs stay exactly where they are. Not sure which version you have? Press the Start button and type About your PC; it's written right there in plain text.

items.title: Columbia County's library pays for Career Online High School — a free, accredited high school diploma you finish from your kitchen table
items.summary: Call the Columbia County Public Library at (386) 758-2111 and ask about Career Online High School. It's a real, accredited high school diploma plus a career certificate, done entirely online at your own pace, and the grant pays the whole cost — you don't pay a dime. The library has a page with the enrollment steps on columbiacountyfla.com (search "Career Online High School" on the site).

items.title: Scammers Fooled a Bank Into Handing Over 50,000 Customers' Private Files
items.summary: Scammers just fooled the online bank Revolut into handing over private files for about 50,000 customers — birth dates, addresses, phone numbers, copies of passports and driver's licenses, even the selfies taken to verify accounts. How? They posed as a government agency using a real government email address, so the request looked completely legitimate. Expect very convincing follow-up scams that quote your real details. Don't trust caller ID or an official-looking email: hang up and call the company back at the number on your card or statement.

items.title: Before you give up on that slow old laptop, look it up on iFixit — free step-by-step guides at ifixit.com
items.summary: iFixit is a free website — ifixit.com — with thousands of step-by-step guides and pictures for bringing laptops and desktops back to life. Look up your machine, see what the job takes, and decide whether it's a 20-minute afternoon job or one for the shop. Parts and small toolkits are sold there too.

items.title: Hard-to-read websites? Firefox's built-in Reader View turns any article into big, clear text — one click, free at firefox.com
items.summary: Firefox is a free web browser, and its Reader View is built right in: when a website is a mess of ads and sidebars, click the page-shaped icon at the right end of the address bar and Reader View strips the page down to plain text. Click the Aa button to make the words bigger, or have the page read aloud to you. Firefox is free at firefox.com.

items.title: Fake Deal Sites Surge After Apple's iPhone Launch — How to Pay Smart
items.summary: Looking for a deal on a hot new gadget? The Guardian warned Sunday about fake shopping sites built to cash in on Apple's new iPhone launch — researchers watched more than 200 copycat websites appear in a single day. They look convincing, and they often insist on payment by bank transfer or digital currency, skipping the protection your card gives you. Buy only from stores you know, pay by credit card, and treat a too-good price as a warning sign. Already paid? Call your bank right away.

items.title: Your inkjet printer dried up again? A Brother laser printer prints on the first try even after months of sitting — Wirecutter's 2026 home-office pick starts around $210 at brother-usa.com
items.summary: Laser printers use toner powder, not liquid ink, so there's nothing to dry out and clog. Wirecutter's 2026 pick for the best home-office laser printer is a Brother — about $210 at brother-usa.com, Best Buy, or Amazon — and a black toner cartridge lasts thousands of pages.

items.title: Homework help for $4 a month — Khan Academy's Khanmigo is an AI tutor that explains instead of answering, at khanmigo.ai
items.summary: Khanmigo is the AI tutor built by Khan Academy, the nonprofit that has offered free school lessons for years. It walks kids through problems step by step instead of doing the work for them. Sign up at khanmigo.ai — $4 a month for families — and the whole library of Khan Academy lessons underneath it stays free.

items.title: Your LG TV reports what you watch to advertisers — turn it off free in Settings > General > System > Advanced Settings > Live Plus
items.summary: A new investigation put it back in the news this week: LG smart TVs record a fingerprint of everything you watch — cable, streaming, even over-the-air — and send it home so advertisers can target you. The fix is one free switch, no account needed: press the Settings (gear) button on the remote, go to General > System > Advanced Settings > Live Plus, and turn it off. On Samsung TVs the similar switch lives under Settings > General > Terms & Privacy.

items.title: Update Chrome, VLC, Zoom, and a dozen apps in one click — Ninite is free at ninite.com
items.summary: Go to ninite.com, check the boxes for the free apps you already use — Chrome, Firefox, VLC, Zoom, and dozens more — and it builds you one installer. Run it once and Ninite installs or updates everything together; no toolbars, no junk offers. Keep that one file on your desktop, run it again about once a month, and every app on the list refreshes itself. Free for home use.

items.title: Scammers Can Fake Your Grandchild's Voice Now — Here's the Family Fix
items.summary: Scammers are calling grandparents in a voice that sounds exactly like their grandchild — because a computer cloned it. The Better Business Bureau warned families this week, just before Grandparents' Day: crooks lift a few seconds of audio and family details from social media, then fake a crash or an arrest and beg for money fast. Hang up and call your grandchild back yourself, and set up a family code word. Then lock your Facebook photos to friends-only — that's where they shop for voices.
